chunks: A number of our companions, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Ali ibn al-Nu'man, from Ali ibn Uqba, from Maysara, who said:

I entered upon Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) while my complexion had changed. He said to me: 'From where did you enter into Ihram?' I said: 'From such and such a place.' He said: 'Often the seeker of goodness stumbles.' Then he said: 'Would it please you if you were to pray Dhuhr during travel as four (rak'cycles')?' I said: 'No.' He said: 'So it is, by Allah, like that.'

key_terms.أَحْرَمْتَ: Entered into the state of Ihram (ritual consecration for Hajj or Umrah)
key_terms.أَرْبَعاً: Four (referring to the number of rak'ats)
key_terms.رُبَّ طَالِبِ خَيْرٍ تَزِلُّ قَدَمُهُ: Often the seeker of goodness stumbles (a proverbial expression used to introduce a legal point)
key_terms.فِي السَّفَرِ: During travel (referring to the ruling of Qasr prayer)
key_terms.مِنْ أَيْنَ: From where (referring to the place of entering Ihram)

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on praying full prayers while in Ihram at a place other than the Miqat?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Al-Kafi* illustrates the principle of *Qiyas* (analogical reasoning) used by Imam al-Sadiq (AS) to determine the ruling of praying full prayers (*Tamam*) at a non-designated Miqat. By comparing the traveler's reluctance to shorten Dhuhr to the reluctance to lengthen it in this specific context, the Imam establishes that praying four rak'ats at a place other than the Miqat is not the standard practice, highlighting the importance of adhering to the prescribed boundaries for Hajj rituals.
